cards.front: How do you get the current process ID in Java?
cards.back: ProcessHandle.current().pid() — the ProcessHandle API arrived in Java 9
cards.extra: Before Java 9 there was no standard API: people parsed the JVM name from ManagementFactory or shelled out to ps.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: What does Objects.requireNonNull(obj) do?
cards.back: Throws NullPointerException immediately if the argument is null, and otherwise returns it for chaining
cards.extra: Because it returns the value, it can be used inline: this.name = Objects.requireNonNull(name); — validation and assignment in one line.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: What is the overload of requireNonNull with a message for?
cards.back: requireNonNull(obj, "name must not be null"), or a Supplier<String> for a lazily built message
cards.extra: The supplier form avoids building the message string on the success path, which matters in hot code.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Which methods does every class inherit from Object?
cards.back: equals, hashCode, toString, getClass, clone, finalize, and the wait/notify/notifyAll trio
cards.extra: getClass is final; wait/notify are final too, which is why locking behaviour cannot be redefined by a subclass.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: How do you convert a ByteBuffer to a byte[]?
cards.back: Read into an array with buffer.get(bytes), or call buffer.array() if hasArray() is true
cards.extra: array() returns the backing store, so it throws for direct buffers and ignores position/limit — copy instead if you need only the remaining bytes.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: How do you wrap a byte[] as a ByteBuffer?
cards.back: ByteBuffer.wrap(bytes) — zero-copy, shares the array
cards.extra: Use ByteBuffer.allocate(n).put(bytes) when you need an independent buffer with its own capacity.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: What does the compiler error "cannot instantiate the type X" mean?
cards.back: You used new on an interface or an abstract class
cards.extra: Both are blueprints. Instantiate a concrete implementation, or an anonymous class if the type has a single method to implement.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Does Java have conditional compilation like #ifdef?
cards.back: No — there is no preprocessor; Java always compiles every branch
cards.extra: The nearest idiom is a static final boolean flag plus an if, which the compiler folds away, leaving dead code that will not compile if it references missing types.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::00 Overview

cards.front: What normally causes javac: package x does not exist?
cards.back: A classpath or module-path problem — the dependency is not where javac looks, not a syntax error
cards.extra: Check that the jar is on -cp, that a modular project puts it on --module-path, and that the package name matches the dependency.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::19 Packages

cards.front: What causes NotSerializableException?
cards.back: The object graph contains a non-transient field whose type is not Serializable
cards.extra: Serialization walks the whole graph, so one bad field anywhere in it fails the write — not just the top-level object.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::17 Serialization

cards.front: How do you serialize an object with a non-serializable field?
cards.back: Mark the field transient, or implement writeObject/readObject to save and restore it manually
cards.extra: Transient means "do not persist"; a custom writeObject means "persist it in another form" — for example as a string or a proxy object.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::17 Serialization

cards.front: Why is a String[] assignable to Object[]?
cards.back: Arrays are covariant — String[] is an Object[]
cards.extra: The array carries its component type at runtime, so storing an Integer into that Object[] throws ArrayStoreException. Generics reject the same code at compile time.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::03 Data Types

cards.front: What does the compile error "capture of ?" mean?
cards.back: A wildcard type was turned into a fresh, unknown type variable, and you tried to use it in a way that requires a specific type
cards.extra: List<?>.add(x) cannot compile: the compiler knows the element type only as "capture#1 of ?". Passing the list to a generic method lets that method capture it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::04 Collections::09 Generics

cards.front: How do you make the JVM prefer IPv4?
cards.back: Run with -Djava.net.preferIPv4Stack=true
cards.extra: The JVM otherwise uses whatever the OS prefers, which on dual-stack hosts is often IPv6 — a common cause of timeouts against IPv4-only services.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::03 Networking in Java

cards.front: How do you copy text to the system clipboard?
cards.back: Toolkit.getDefaultToolkit().getSystemClipboard().setContents(new StringSelection(text), null)
cards.extra: The AWT clipboard works from console applications too, though it needs a display on Linux; DataFlavor.stringFlavor is the format used.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::16 Swing GUI

cards.front: Does Java have function pointers?
cards.back: No — but functional interfaces plus method references give the same capability
cards.extra: Function<Integer,Integer> f = Math::abs; stores behaviour in a variable and passes it around. The difference is that the target type must be a functional interface.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces

cards.front: What is Objects.requireNonNullElse for?
cards.back: Returning the first argument if it is non-null, otherwise the second — a null-safe default
cards.extra: It replaces the x != null ? x : default idiom, and the default must itself be non-null.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: How do you write multi-paragraph Javadoc?
cards.back: Use <p> to open each new paragraph and keep the first sentence as a summary
cards.extra: Blank lines alone do not create paragraphs in a doc comment; the HTML tag is what does it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::12 Documentation::02 Javadoc

cards.front: What is the Java Class-File API?
cards.back: java.lang.classfile — a standard API for parsing and generating class files, final in Java 24 (JEP 484)
cards.extra: It replaces the internal ASM-based machinery the JDK used for its own tools, so bytecode tools can drop a third-party dependency.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: What is the standard way to store 2D coordinates in modern Java?
cards.back: A record Point(double x, double y)
cards.extra: A record gives you a named type, value equality, toString, and immutability with one line — far better than two loose ints or a double[].
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: What released in Java 25?
cards.back: The next LTS release (September 2025) — language, library and runtime updates including flexible constructor bodies
cards.extra: LTS releases are the ones enterprises adopt; feature releases in between get 6 months of support.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals
